AI.method: APVI-SLAM introduces: (1) a reliability-aware localization framework that dynamically reweights sensor estimators; (2) a sliding-window freezing strategy to recover from tracking failures; (3) an efficient quadtree-guided mapping module for incremental water-medium modeling and 3D Gaussian optimization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on public benchmarks and a proposed coral reef surveying dataset demonstrate that APVI-SLAM achieves state-of-the-art localization and reconstruction quality at real-time speeds.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes both the APVI-SLAM system and a coral reef surveying benchmark dataset with synchronized multi-modality data, providing a comprehensive solution for underwater SLAM with robustness against visual failures.

title: RoboVAST: Automated Scenario-Based Validation of Robots at Scale
summary: Validation of robotic systems critically depends on the operating conditions under which they are assessed. Scenario selection and variation are often manual, experience-driven, and difficult to scale, which harms reproducibility and weakens validation conclusions. We propose a scenario-based methodology that models scenarios compositionally and formalizes how these dimensions are varied, instantiated, executed, and interpreted. Building on this, we introduce RoboVAST, a framework that realizes declarative campaign specifications, plugin-based scenario generation, and scalable containerized execution with integrated result analysis. We demonstrate the approach with a navigation dataset comprising 5480 scenario configurations and over 100000 execution runs across five indoor maps with varied paths, sensor noise, software parameters, and obstacle settings, totaling more than 1800 hours of simulated operation and 1873 km traveled. Twenty repetitions per configuration allow us to distinguish systematic failures from stochastic anomalies.

AI.tldr: RoboVAST is a framework for scalable validation of robotic systems through declarative scenario specifications, plugin-based generation, and containerized execution with integrated result analysis.
AI.motivation: Validation of robotic systems depends on operating conditions, but current scenario selection and variation methods are manual, experience-driven, difficult to scale, and lead to poor reproducibility and weak validation conclusions.
AI.method: A scenario-based methodology that models scenarios compositionally and formalizes dimensions of variation, instantiation, execution, and interpretation. RoboVAST implements this through declarative campaign specifications, plugin-based scenario generation, and scalable containerized execution with integrated result analysis.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a navigation dataset of 5,480 scenario configurations, over 100,000 execution runs across five indoor maps with varied paths, sensor noise, software parameters, and obstacle settings, totaling 1,800+ hours of simulated operation and 1,873 km traveled. Twenty repetitions per configuration enabled distinguishing systematic failures from stochastic anomalies.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables scalable, reproducible validation of robotic systems by formalizing scenario composition and variation, addressing the limitations of manual, experience-driven approaches to system validation.

title: Diagnosing Semantic Handoff Failures in Agent-Orchestrated Vision-Language-Action Skill Composition
summary: Long-horizon household tasks require robots to compose many language-conditioned skills, yet the boundary between consecutive skills is rarely explicit. A skill may satisfy its own postcondition while leaving the robot, objects, or camera views in a state from which the next skill cannot reliably start. We study this semantic handoff problem in BEHAVIOR-1K through an agent-orchestrated vision-language-action execution harness. The harness invokes $π_{0.5}$-based skill checkpoints trained from cleaned BEHAVIOR-1K demonstrations, assigns each skill typed arguments and a step budget, and uses multi-view vision-language model verification to decide whether execution should advance, retry, or replan. To separate isolated skill competence from long-horizon compositional robustness, we evaluate the same checkpoints under two initial-state distributions: clean skill-boundary snapshots and chained terminal states produced by previous skills. Selected navigation, grasping, placement, and door-opening skills achieve 77--100% success from clean snapshots under human-reviewed verification, yet composed rollouts still frequently stall from chained states. Execution traces attribute these failures to next-skill readiness, target grounding, and low-level control execution, revealing a substantial gap between single-skill success and reliable long-horizon task completion. These findings turn near-zero end-to-end task success into actionable diagnostics, showing that future VLA skill libraries must learn robustness to the messy chained-state distribution that clean demonstrations systematically underrepresent.

AI.tldr: The authors study the semantic handoff problem in long-horizon household tasks using BEHAVIOR-1K, demonstrating a substantial gap between single-skill success (77-100%) and reliable long-horizon task completion due to issues with skill boundaries and chained states.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon household tasks require robots to compose many language-conditioned skills, yet the boundary between consecutive skills is rarely explicit. A skill may satisfy its own postcondition while leaving the robot, objects, or camera views in a state from which the next skill cannot reliably start. This semantic handoff problem prevents reliable long-horizon task completion.
AI.method: An agent-orchestrated vision-language-action execution harness that invokes π0.5-based skill checkpoints from cleaned BEHAVIOR-1K demonstrations, assigns typed arguments and step budgets, and uses multi-view vision-language model verification to decide execution progression (advance, retry, or replan). The evaluation compares the same checkpoints under two initial-state distributions: clean skill-boundary snapshots and chained terminal states from previous skills.
AI.result: Selected navigation, grasping, placement, and door-opening skills achieve 77-100% success from clean snapshots under human-reviewed verification. However, composed rollouts frequently stall from chained states, with failures attributed to next-skill readiness, target grounding, and low-level control execution. The findings reveal a substantial gap between single-skill success and reliable long-horizon task completion.
AI.conclusion: Near-zero end-to-end task success reveals actionable diagnostics. Future vision-language-action (VLA) skill libraries must learn robustness to the messy chained-state distribution that clean demonstrations systematically underrepresent. The semantic handoff problem is a critical challenge for achieving reliable long-horizon task completion with compositional skill libraries.

title: Optimal Transport Q-Learning for Flow Policy Steering and Acceleration
summary: Diffusion and flow policies have recently demonstrated remarkable performance in robotic applications by accurately capturing multimodal robot trajectory distributions, especially in the context of vision language action (VLA) models. However, high quality policy performance also requires fast inference and high quality demonstrations, which are often hard to get. Lack of these leads to suboptimal policy behaviors and failure under distribution shifts. In this work we address the problem of fine-tuning and accelerating suboptimal flow-based policies using the robot's experience through RL post-training. We introduce Optimal Transport Q-Learning (OTQL), a new method for finetuning flow policies using advantage weighted conditional optimal transport flow matching. OTQL can finetune and accelerate flows with an interaction budget of 50-60 episodes while avoiding computationally expensive distillation in simulation and real-world robot tasks. Our results show that OTQL post-trains flow policies using the robot's own experience, increasing average success percentage of single-task policies from 36% to 86% and of a pre-trained VLA from 38% to 76% while reducing the number of inference steps per action generation by 70%.

AI.tldr: OTQL is a method that fine-tunes and accelerates suboptimal flow-based robotic policies using only 50-60 episodes of robot experience via advantage weighted conditional optimal transport flow matching, improving success rates from 36-86% (single-task) and 38-76% (pre-trained VLA) while reducing inference steps by 70%.
AI.motivation: Flow policies perform well in capturing multimodal robot trajectory distributions but require fast inference and high-quality demonstrations which are often unavailable. Lack of these leads to suboptimal policy behaviors and failures under distribution shifts.
AI.method: Optimal Transport Q-Learning (OTQL) uses advantage weighted conditional optimal transport flow matching to fine-tune and accelerate flow policies using only the robot's own experience, avoiding computationally expensive distillation in simulation or real-world tasks.
AI.result: OTQL post-trains flow policies with an interaction budget of 50-60 episodes, increasing average success percentage from 36% to 86% for single-task policies and from 38% to 76% for pre-trained VLA models, while reducing the number of inference steps per action generation by 70%.
AI.conclusion: OTQL successfully enables fine-tuning and acceleration of flow policies using only robot experience, demonstrating that high-quality policy performance can be achieved without expensive distillation processes in either simulation or real-world environments.

title: LAMP: Latent Motion Prior-Guided Real-World Learning for Dexterous Hand Manipulation
summary: Real-world learning for dexterous hands remains brittle because high-dimensional hand actions amplify imitation errors and make reinforcement-learning exploration prone to contact-breaking motion. While combining imitation learning (IL) with online reinforcement learning (RL) can reduce manual supervision, unconstrained exploration in raw hand-action spaces is sample-inefficient and risky for physical hardware. We introduce a latent motion prior module (\prior{}) that maps recent hand-action histories to a compact, history-conditioned latent prior and decodes continuous latent commands into executable high-dimensional hand targets. Built on this prior, \method{} is a three-stage real-world dexterous learning framework: it pretrains \prior{} from demonstrations, trains a visuomotor policy that predicts native arm commands and latent hand-action offsets, and improves the policy with online residual RL in the same latent hand-action space. This shared, decodable interface lets residual exploration make local corrections near demonstrated, contact-consistent hand motions rather than perturbing every finger joint independently. We evaluate \method{} on four real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks against raw, linear, and discrete hand-action interfaces. Starting from small task-specific demonstration sets, \method{} achieves a 56.25\% average IL success rate and raises it to 98.75\% after online RL, reaching 100\% final success on three tasks and 95\% on the remaining task.

AI.tldr: A three-stage framework combining imitation learning with online residual reinforcement learning in a latent hand-action space, using a latent motion prior module to enable efficient exploration and high success rates on real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Real-world dexterous hand learning is brittle due to high-dimensional action spaces amplifying imitation errors and making RL exploration prone to contact-breaking. While IL+RL reduces manual supervision, raw hand-action exploration is sample-inefficient and risky for physical hardware.
AI.method: Introduces a latent motion prior module that maps hand-action histories to a compact, history-conditioned latent prior and decodes continuous latent commands into high-dimensional hand targets. The three-stage framework: (1) pretrains the prior from demonstrations, (2) trains a visuomotor policy predicting arm commands and latent hand-action offsets, (3) improves policy with online residual RL in the latent space.
AI.result: Evaluated on four real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks. Starting from small demonstration sets, achieved 56.25% IL success rate and raised it to 98.75% after online RL, reaching 100% success on three tasks and 95% on the remaining task, outperforming raw, linear, and discrete hand-action interfaces.
AI.conclusion: The shared, decodable latent interface enables residual exploration to make local corrections near demonstrated, contact-consistent hand motions rather than perturbing every finger joint independently, achieving robust dexterous manipulation with minimal demonstration data.

title: OrchardBench: A Physically-Grounded, GPU-Parallel Apple-Orchard Simulation Benchmark for Agricultural Robotics
summary: Robotic tree-fruit harvesting is a flagship problem for agricultural automation, but progress is bottlenecked by the cost and irreproducibility of field experiments: an orchard is available only weeks a year, every tree is different, and a control error can permanently damage the crop or the plant. The tree models used in graphics and agronomy are geometrically detailed but physically inert, while the GPU-parallel simulators used in robot learning contain no plausible trees. We present OrchardBench, a physically-grounded, GPU-parallel simulation of apple-orchard trees on the Newton engine. Each tree is grown by a stochastic L-system and instantiated as a fully articulated body: branches are compliant torsional spring-dampers whose stiffness follows Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, they break at a wood modulus of rupture and fall as free hinges, and apples are independent bodies on stem tethers that detach at literature-grounded pull forces and load the branch when pulled. A moving, density-controllable foliage layer occludes the canopy as real leaves do. Every physical parameter is tied to a published source. Per-environment domain randomization makes each batched world a distinct tree, and a mobile manipulator with a wrist depth camera closes the loop with geometric fruit perception and an autonomous harvesting baseline. Careful engineering of the solver and the model lets OrchardBench run many parallel environments at interactive rates on a laptop GPU. We define the tasks and a metric suite spanning harvest completeness, throughput, and plant damage (with a per-canopy-zone breakdown), and report baseline results across foliage, fruit load, terrain, canopy zone, and parallelism. The analytic baseline succeeds on about 40% of the fruit it detects and harvests only about an eighth of the reachable fruit on a tree, leaving clear headroom for novel autonomy approaches.

AI.tldr: OrchardBench is a physically-grounded, GPU-parallel simulation of apple-orchard trees for robotic harvesting research, addressing the cost and irreproducibility of field experiments.
AI.motivation: Robotic tree-fruit harvesting is a flagship agricultural automation problem, but progress is bottlenecked by the cost and irreproducibility of field experiments: orchards are available only weeks per year, every tree is different, and control errors can permanently damage crops or plants. Existing tree models lack physical properties, and robot learning simulators contain no plausible trees.
AI.method: OrchardBench is built on the Newton engine and features: stochastic L-system tree growth, fully articulated tree bodies with Euler-Bernoulli beam theory compliant torsional spring-dampers, branches that break at wood modulus of rupture and fall as free hinges, apples as independent bodies on stem tethers that detach at literature-grounded pull forces, density-controllable foliage layer for realistic canopy occlusion, per-environment domain randomization, and a mobile manipulator with wrist depth camera for geometric fruit perception.
AI.result: The analytic baseline succeeds on about 40% of the fruit it detects and harvests only about an eighth of the reachable fruit on a tree. The platform enables evaluation across multiple dimensions: harvest completeness, throughput, and plant damage (with per-canopy-zone breakdown), across foliage, fruit load, terrain, canopy zone, and parallelism configurations.
AI.conclusion: OrchardBench provides a scalable simulation platform for autonomous harvesting research with careful solver engineering enabling interactive rates on laptop GPUs. The clear performance gap (baseline achieves only ~12.5% of reachable fruit) leaves substantial headroom for novel autonomy approaches, making it an effective tool for accelerating research before costly field experiments.

title: Responsible Personalisation: The Double-Edged Sword of Personalisation in Human-Robot Interaction
summary: While personalisation is becoming a defining capability in human-robot interaction (HRI), the existing literature on responsible personalisation remains fragmented, offering isolated accounts of ethical risks without a structured understanding of how they emerge across interaction contexts. This gap is particularly critical in HRI, where robots' embodiment and social presence can amplify and reshape such risks or generate new types of risks. We present a lifecycle-based and context-sensitive framework for personalised HRI, grounded in an embodiment-aware perspective. The framework combines stages of the personalisation process with interaction characteristics (short-term vs. long-term, open-domain vs. closed-domain), enabling systematic analysis of how risks arise and evolve. Building on this, we conduct an integrative analysis of key ethical risks, including autonomy erosion, biased user modelling, manipulation, dehumanisation, and privacy violations, and examine how they manifest across contexts. We translate these insights into actionable design recommendations and outline open research challenges. By structuring both the design space and risk landscape of personalised HRI, this work provides a foundation for more systematic, transparent, and ethically grounded approaches to personalised robot behaviour.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a lifecycle-based, context-sensitive framework for personalized human-robot interaction (HRI) that systematically analyzes ethical risks (autonomy erosion, biased user modeling, manipulation, dehumanisation, privacy violations) across different interaction contexts, providing actionable design recommendations.
AI.motivation: Existing literature on responsible personalization in HRI is fragmented, offering isolated accounts of ethical risks without a structured understanding of how they emerge across interaction contexts. The unique challenge in HRI is that robots' embodiment and social presence can amplify, reshape, or generate new types of ethical risks compared to other domains.
AI.method: The authors develop a framework combining stages of the personalization process (lifecycle-based) with interaction characteristics (short-term vs. long-term, open-domain vs. closed-domain). They conduct an integrative analysis of five key ethical risks (autonomy erosion, biased user modeling, manipulation, dehumanisation, and privacy violations) and examine how these manifest across different contexts. The framework enables systematic analysis of how risks arise and evolve throughout the personalization lifecycle.
AI.result: The framework successfully structures both the design space and risk landscape of personalized HRI. The analysis reveals how ethical risks emerge and evolve across different interaction contexts and personalization stages. The authors translate these insights into actionable design recommendations for creating more systematic, transparent, and ethically grounded personalized robot behaviors.
AI.conclusion: By providing a structured foundation for understanding ethical risks in personalized HRI, this work enables designers and researchers to systematically address ethical considerations throughout the personalization lifecycle. The framework helps bridge the gap between isolated ethical risk accounts and a comprehensive understanding of how risks emerge across contexts, ultimately supporting more responsible and ethically grounded HRI systems.

title: Training-Free Acceleration for Vision-Language-Action Models with Action Caching and Refinement
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach for generalizable robotic manipulations. In particular, flow matching-based VLA models have shown remarkable success due to their capability to generate precise and smooth action sequences and capture multimodal distributions. However, the iterative denoising process in the action head acts as a major computational bottleneck, posing a critical challenge for real-time deployment. To address this challenge, we propose ActionCache, a plug-and-play external cache that opportunistically reuses past intermediate actions to warm-start generations from the vicinity of target actions, thereby drastically reducing the inference latency. Specifically, ActionCache stores the intermediate actions with compact multimodal keys, which enables retrieval from similar past contexts across different episodes or even different tasks. Experimental results in simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that ActionCache maintains high task success rates in a low-latency regime, achieving inference acceleration of up to $11.75\times$ and $34.43\times$ for representative flow-based VLA models, $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T-N1.6, respectively.

AI.tldr: ActionCache is a plug-and-play external cache that reuses past intermediate actions to warm-start generation, reducing inference latency for flow-based VLA models by up to 34.43× while maintaining high task success rates.
AI.motivation: Flow matching-based VLA models generate precise action sequences but suffer from an iterative denoising process in the action head that creates a major computational bottleneck, making real-time deployment challenging.
AI.method: ActionCache stores intermediate actions with compact multimodal keys, enabling retrieval from similar past contexts across different episodes or tasks to warm-start generation near target actions.
AI.result: Experimental results show ActionCache achieves up to 11.75× acceleration for π₀.₅ and 34.43× for GR00T-N1.6 while maintaining high task success rates in a low-latency regime.
AI.conclusion: ActionCache effectively addresses the computational bottleneck of flow-based VLA models by reusing past actions, enabling real-time deployment with significant inference acceleration without sacrificing task performance.

title: Towards Real-World Applications with an Autonomous Powered Wheelchair
summary: Wheelchair users call for assistive mobility systems that provide active support, adapt to dynamic environments, and are intuitive and user-friendly. However, powered wheelchairs typically still provide limited autonomy and lack effective integration with advanced perception and navigation capabilities, particularly in complex real-world environments. This paper presents a preliminary study toward autonomous powered wheelchairs for real-world assistive mobility. We introduce a proof-of-concept prototype that integrates autonomous perception, gesture-based interaction, and navigation on a commercially available self-balancing powered wheelchair. The proposed system builds upon Genny Zero, a commercial self-balancing wheelchair that enables hands-free and intuitive operation through body-weight shifting. To extend its capabilities toward autonomous operation, we integrate an RGB-D camera for human-aware perception and interaction, together with a LiDAR sensor for localization and navigation. We demonstrate the integrated system in two assistive applications: (i) hailing, allowing users to call the wheelchair from a distance; and (ii) people-following, where the wheelchair follows a person using leader-follower strategies, including a constrained indoor navigation example. The results highlight the potential of combining autonomous robotics with assistive mobility platforms, while also showing the feasibility of the proposed integration and identifying the main technical challenges that must be addressed before moving toward user-ready, accessible, and intelligent mobility solutions. A video demonstrating the experimental setup and results is available at: https://youtu.be/LVAix_Qx7bM.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a proof-of-concept prototype that integrates autonomous perception, gesture-based interaction, and navigation onto a commercially available self-balancing powered wheelchair (Genny Zero). The system demonstrates two assistive applications: hailing (calling the wheelchair from a distance) and people-following using leader-follower strategies, including a constrained indoor navigation example.
AI.motivation: Wheelchair users require assistive mobility systems that provide active support, adapt to dynamic environments, and are intuitive and user-friendly. However, powered wheelchairs typically have limited autonomy and lack effective integration with advanced perception and navigation capabilities, particularly in complex real-world environments.
AI.method: The researchers integrated an RGB-D camera for human-aware perception and interaction, together with a LiDAR sensor for localization and navigation, onto a Genny Zero self-balancing wheelchair. The system implements two assistive applications: (i) hailing, allowing users to call the wheelchair from a distance, and (ii) people-following using leader-follower strategies, including a constrained indoor navigation example.
AI.result: The results demonstrate the potential of combining autonomous robotics with assistive mobility platforms and show the feasibility of the proposed integration. The study identifies main technical challenges that must be addressed before developing user-ready, accessible, and intelligent mobility solutions.
AI.conclusion: The preliminary study successfully demonstrates that integrating autonomous robotics with assistive mobility platforms is feasible. While the results show promising potential, the authors identify key technical challenges that need to be resolved to develop user-ready solutions, highlighting the need for further research in this area.

title: Learning to Throw Objects Safely in Multi-Obstacle Environments
comment: This paper has been presented at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics & Automation (ICRA), 2026
summary: Robotic throwing enables fast and efficient object placement beyond the robot's immediate workspace, but reliable throwing in cluttered environments remains underexplored. Existing approaches, such as TossingBot, learn throwing strategies from visual input but assume obstacle-free settings. In this paper, we address the problem of throwing objects into a target basket while avoiding obstacles placed randomly in the scene. We introduce a potential field state representation that compactly encodes both basket attraction and obstacle repulsion on a fixed-size grid, enabling reinforcement learning (RL) policies to generalize across arbitrary numbers and configurations of obstacles. The policy is initialized from kinesthetic demonstrations and optimized in simulation using three state-of-the-art RL algorithms (SAC, DDPG, TD3). Among these, SAC achieves the most consistent performance across scenarios. We compare the potential field representation against explicit state encodings and demonstrate that it achieves higher success rates and better scalability to unseen obstacle configurations. Real-robot experiments with unseen throwable objects confirm robust sim-to-real transfer, achieving up to $90\%$ success in cluttered scenes. These results demonstrate that PFR provides a practical and robust representation for safe and efficient robotic throwing in unstructured environments. A video showcasing our experiments is available at: https://youtu.be/ZZnJf8ua2dE

AI.tldr: A reinforcement learning approach using potential field state representation enables robotic throwing with obstacle avoidance, achieving 90% success rate in cluttered environments through sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing robotic throwing systems like TossingBot cannot handle cluttered environments with obstacles. While throwing enables efficient object placement beyond the robot's immediate workspace, reliable throwing in cluttered settings remains underexplored. The authors aim to develop a system that can throw objects into a target basket while avoiding randomly placed obstacles.
AI.method: The paper introduces a potential field state representation that encodes basket attraction and obstacle repulsion on a fixed-size grid. This representation enables reinforcement learning (RL) policies to generalize across arbitrary numbers and configurations of obstacles. The policy is initialized from kinesthetic demonstrations and optimized in simulation using three RL algorithms: SAC (Soft Actor-Critic), DDPG (Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient), and TD3 (Twin Delayed DDPG). The approach is compared against explicit state encodings to demonstrate its advantages.
AI.result: Among the three RL algorithms tested, SAC achieves the most consistent performance across scenarios. The potential field representation outperforms explicit state encodings, achieving higher success rates and better scalability to unseen obstacle configurations. Real-robot experiments with unseen throwable objects demonstrate robust sim-to-real transfer, achieving up to 90% success rate in cluttered scenes.
AI.conclusion: The potential field representation (PFR) provides a practical and robust representation for safe and efficient robotic throwing in unstructured environments. The approach successfully addresses the challenge of throwing with obstacle avoidance and shows strong generalization capabilities to novel scenarios.

title: From Foundation to Application: Improving VLA Models in Practice
summary: Despite recent progress of VLA foundation models, the disparity between laboratory conditions and real-world applications continues to impede their practical implementation. To bridge this gap, we present LingBot-VLA 2.0, which advances LingBot-VLA through improvements in three functional domains. (1) Generalization across tasks and embodiments. Compared to the previous version, we revamp the data processing pipeline and curate around 60,000 hours of data for pretraining, including 50,000 hours of robot trajectories spanning 20 robot configurations and 10,000 hours of egocentric human videos. (2) Expanded action space in addition to dual-arm hardware platforms. In particular, our system accommodates degrees of freedom for the heads, waists, mobile bases, and dexterous hands, thereby empowering the robots to tackle more complex tasks in practical scenarios. (3) Predictive dynamics modeling for improved temporal reasoning. Specifically, we formulate future prediction as a proxy task, facilitated by a video representation model for semantic priors and a depth estimation model for geometric cues. Evaluations on the GM-100 benchmark, conducted in a generalist setting, validate the beneficial impact of these proposed modifications. Furthermore, benefiting from the expanded pretraining data that covers whole-body degrees of freedom, LingBot-VLA-2.0 demonstrates strong cross-embodiment long-horizon mobile manipulation capability across the two robotic platforms.

AI.tldr: LingBot-VLA 2.0 advances VLA foundation models by improving generalization across tasks/embodiments, expanding the action space to include whole-body degrees of freedom (heads, waists, mobile bases, dexterous hands), and incorporating predictive dynamics modeling for enhanced temporal reasoning, demonstrating strong cross-embodiment long-horizon mobile manipulation capabilities.
AI.motivation: Despite recent progress in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models, a significant gap remains between laboratory conditions and real-world applications, hindering practical implementation.
AI.method: Three functional domain improvements: (1) Generalization enhancement via revamped data pipeline with ~60,000 hours of pretraining data (50,000 hours of robot trajectories across 20 configurations and 10,000 hours of egocentric human videos); (2) Expanded action space to support dual-arm hardware plus heads, waists, mobile bases, and dexterous hands; (3) Predictive dynamics modeling using video representation models for semantic priors and depth estimation models for geometric cues to facilitate temporal reasoning.
AI.result: Evaluations on the GM-100 benchmark in a generalist setting confirm the beneficial impact of proposed modifications. The model demonstrates strong cross-embodiment long-horizon mobile manipulation capability across two robotic platforms.
AI.conclusion: The proposed modifications successfully bridge the gap between lab conditions and real-world applications, validating the effectiveness of enhanced generalization, expanded action space, and predictive dynamics modeling for practical VLA deployment.

title: SIEVE: Structure-Aware Data Selection for Imitation Learning with VLA Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained by imitation learning on large-scale robot demonstration datasets, but more data does not necessarily yield better policies due to redundancy, noise, and uneven coverage. Existing data selection methods often assess demonstrations at either the trajectory or state-action level, missing the reusable structures that compose long-horizon behaviors. In this paper, we propose SIEVE, a structure-aware data selection method for VLA imitation learning. SIEVE views demonstrations as compositions of reusable primitives and transition interfaces. It first discovers visuo-motor primitives from segmented trajectories, then allocates selection budgets to composition patterns by maximizing reuse-aware structural exposure under diminishing returns. Finally, it selects medoid trajectories within each composition-pattern bucket to retain central, stable, and imitation-friendly demonstrations. Experiments across multiple datasets, benchmarks, and VLA models show that SIEVE consistently outperforms competitive data selection baselines. Notably, SIEVE can surpass full-data training while using only 50% of demonstrations and 50% of training steps, suggesting that reusable structure, captured through primitives and transitions, is an important signal for efficient VLA imitation learning.

AI.tldr: SIEVE is a structure-aware data selection method for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) imitation learning that discovers reusable visuo-motor primitives and transition interfaces from demonstrations, allocates selection budgets based on reuse-aware structural exposure under diminishing returns, and selects medoid trajectories within composition pattern buckets. It consistently outperforms competitive baselines across multiple datasets and VLA models, achieving performance comparable to full-data training with only 50% of demonstrations and training steps.
AI.motivation: VLA models trained via imitation learning on large-scale robot demonstration datasets suffer from redundancy, noise, and uneven coverage. Existing data selection methods evaluate demonstrations at trajectory or state-action levels, missing the reusable structures that compose long-horizon behaviors, which limits the effectiveness of data selection for efficient VLA imitation learning.
AI.method: SIEVE views demonstrations as compositions of reusable primitives and transition interfaces. The method proceeds in three stages: (1) discovers visuo-motor primitives from segmented trajectories, (2) allocates selection budgets to composition patterns by maximizing reuse-aware structural exposure under diminishing returns, and (3) selects medoid trajectories within each composition-pattern bucket to retain central, stable, and imitation-friendly demonstrations.
AI.result: SIEVE consistently outperforms competitive data selection baselines across multiple datasets, benchmarks, and VLA models. Notably, SIEVE can surpass full-data training while using only 50% of demonstrations and 50% of training steps, demonstrating superior efficiency in data selection for VLA imitation learning.
AI.conclusion: Reusable structure, captured through primitives and transitions, is an important signal for efficient VLA imitation learning. By identifying and leveraging these structural components, SIEVE enables more effective data selection that can match or exceed full-data performance with significantly reduced data and computational resources.

title: Hilti-Trimble-Oxford Dataset: 360 Visual-Inertial Benchmark with Floor Plan Priors for SLAM and Localization
summary: Automated progress monitoring on construction sites is an active area of research and development. Robot and human-carried mapping systems have been developed to build 3D maps of building and infrastructure projects. While LiDAR-based mapping systems achieve high accuracy, the cost of LiDAR can be prohibitive. Consumer-grade cameras with wide field of view ("360 cameras") combined with embedded inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide a cost-effective alternative. To support change detection and progress monitoring, highly accurate visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) and floor plan-referenced localization systems are required. In this paper we present a high-quality dataset collected at an active construction site, which captures realistic challenges such as variable lighting conditions, moving workers, fast motions, and repetitive structures. The dataset offers thirty visual-inertial sequences recorded across seven floors over an eight-month period of the construction project. Ground truth trajectories were collected using a high quality LiDAR-inertial SLAM system rigidly attached to the 360 camera. Additionally, we report the results of an open research challenge evaluating the best visual SLAM and localization systems from around the world. The Challenge attracted substantially higher participation in SLAM, with 62 teams compared to 22 in floor-plan-referenced localization, reflecting the broader maturity of SLAM methods. The higher errors in localization further highlight the difficulty of this task in construction and point to the need for continued research, which this dataset is intended to support. The dataset and the benchmark are publicly available at: https://hilti-trimble-challenge.com/dataset-2026.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a high-quality visual-inertial dataset and benchmark for automated progress monitoring on construction sites, featuring 30 sequences across 7 floors collected over 8 months, along with results from an international SLAM and floor plan-referenced localization challenge.
AI.motivation: LiDAR-based mapping systems achieve high accuracy for construction site monitoring but are prohibitively expensive. Consumer-grade cameras with IMUs offer a cost-effective alternative, but they require highly accurate visual SLAM and floor plan-referenced localization systems. Existing datasets lack realistic construction challenges such as variable lighting, moving workers, fast motions, and repetitive structures.
AI.method: The authors collected a dataset at an active construction site capturing 30 visual-inertial sequences across 7 floors over 8 months, including realistic challenges like variable lighting, moving workers, fast motions, and repetitive structures. Ground truth trajectories were collected using a high-quality LiDAR-inertial SLAM system rigidly attached to the 360 camera. An open research challenge was conducted to evaluate the best visual SLAM and floor plan-referenced localization systems from around the world.
AI.result: The challenge attracted 62 teams for SLAM and 22 teams for floor plan-referenced localization, demonstrating broader maturity of SLAM methods. Higher localization errors compared to SLAM highlighted the significant difficulty of floor plan-referenced localization in construction environments.
AI.conclusion: The publicly available dataset (https://hilti-trimble-challenge.com/dataset-2026) and benchmark support continued research to improve localization accuracy for automated construction progress monitoring, particularly for floor plan-referenced localization which remains challenging due to construction-specific complexities.

title: Clustering-Embedded Model Predictive Path Integral Control: Avoiding Averaging-Induced Failure and Enabling Efficient Cluster Selection for Dynamic Obstacles
summary: With the widespread availability of parallel computing hardware, sampling-based motion planning methods such as Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control have become increasingly powerful for complex nonlinear systems in non-smooth task spaces. However, the sampling and forward-simulation pipeline in MPPI suffers from averaging-induced failure in cluttered environments, where the importance-weighted update averages incompatible rollouts and leads to hesitation or even collision when an obstacle lies directly ahead. This paper proposes Clustering-Embedded MPPI (CE-MPPI), a framework that architecturally resolves the averaging-induced failures inherent in standard MPPI within non-convex environments. Rather than simply mitigating interference, CE-MPPI redefines the control law by integrating a high-fidelity pruning and clustering stage. By leveraging density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) alongside a novel geometric direction feature that is extracted from collision-derived reference points, the system isolates feasible trajectory modes from the noise of infeasible rollouts. This is paired with an intelligent selection logic that optimizes for minimum cost in static scenes while actively steering opposite to obstacle flux in dynamic environments. Experiments in 2-D JAX-accelerated simulations show that CE-MPPI alleviates obstacle-front hesitation and avoids persistent coupling with moving obstacles in dynamic scenes. In particular, real-world tests on a 6-DoF UR5e manipulator with CUDA-parallel rollouts in Isaac Gym achieve a 48\% reduction in time-to-goal and a 12\% shorter end-effector path.

AI.tldr: CE-MPPI is a motion planning framework that addresses averaging-induced failures in standard Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control by integrating DBSCAN clustering and geometric direction features to isolate feasible trajectory modes from infeasible rollouts, achieving 48% faster task completion and 12% shorter path on a UR5e manipulator.
AI.motivation: Standard MPPI suffers from averaging-induced failures in cluttered environments where the importance-weighted update averages incompatible rollouts, causing hesitation or collision when obstacles lie directly ahead.
AI.method: CE-MPPI redefines the control law by integrating a high-fidelity pruning and clustering stage that uses DBSCAN for density-based spatial clustering of trajectory rollouts, extracts a novel geometric direction feature from collision-derived reference points, and implements intelligent selection logic optimizing for minimum cost in static scenes while actively steering opposite to obstacle flux in dynamic environments.
AI.result: Experiments in 2-D JAX-accelerated simulations and real-world tests on a 6-DoF UR5e manipulator with CUDA-parallel rollouts in Isaac Gym show CE-MPPI alleviates obstacle-front hesitation and avoids persistent coupling with moving obstacles, achieving 48% reduction in time-to-goal and 12% shorter end-effector path compared to standard MPPI.
AI.conclusion: Clustering-Embedded MPPI architecturally resolves averaging-induced failures in non-convex environments by isolating feasible trajectory modes through DBSCAN clustering and geometric direction features, demonstrating significant performance improvements in both static and dynamic scenarios.

title: Hypothesis-driven Model Expansion under Uncertainty for Open-World Robot Planning
comment: Accepted to Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS) 2026
summary: We consider an open-world planning setting in which service robots must operate in unknown environments with incomplete knowledge of objects and actions. Traditional closed-world approaches with pre-programmed knowledge bases fail when robots encounter unexpected situations and tasks, posing a fundamental challenge for autonomous knowledge expansion in human environments. In this work, we propose an open-world planning framework that enables robots to automatically generate, verify, and update hypotheses about their abstract world models. Our key insight is to explicitly maintain uncertainty-aware knowledge expansion and integrate hypothesis verification into goal-reaching planning. The framework leverages foundation models to generate initial hypotheses over states and transitions, and applies automated planning to produce action sequences that jointly address hypothesis verification and task execution. Through iterative execution and refinement, the robot expands its knowledge by incorporating verification feedback from the foundation models when hypotheses prove incorrect. Extensive experiments in simulated and real-world environments demonstrate that our framework enables autonomous knowledge expansion and effective operation in open-world settings. These results indicate that integrating uncertainty-aware model expansion from robot foundation models with planning advances the practical deployment of household service robots.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an open-world planning framework for service robots that automatically generates, verifies, and updates hypotheses about world models by integrating foundation models with automated planning, enabling autonomous knowledge expansion in unknown environments.
AI.motivation: Traditional closed-world approaches with pre-programmed knowledge bases fail when robots encounter unexpected situations and tasks in unknown environments, posing a fundamental challenge for autonomous knowledge expansion in human environments.
AI.method: The framework explicitly maintains uncertainty-aware knowledge expansion and integrates hypothesis verification into goal-reaching planning. It leverages foundation models to generate initial hypotheses over states and transitions, applies automated planning to produce action sequences for joint hypothesis verification and task execution, and uses iterative execution with verification feedback from foundation models to refine hypotheses when they prove incorrect.
AI.result: Extensive experiments in both simulated and real-world environments demonstrate that the framework enables autonomous knowledge expansion and effective operation in open-world settings.
AI.conclusion: Integrating uncertainty-aware model expansion from robot foundation models with planning advances the practical deployment of household service robots.

title: Neural-ESO: A Dual-Pathway Architecture for Provably Robust Learning-Based Control
summary: A learning-enabled disturbance-rejection framework based on a Neural Extended State Observer (Neural-ESO) is presented in this letter. Unlike existing learning-based control methods that largely rely on the learned model once deployed, Neural-ESO adopts a dual-pathway architecture: a predictive pathway uses a neural network to provide a feedforward disturbance estimate that accelerates convergence, while a corrective pathway employs a conventional ESO to compensate prediction errors and prevent over-reliance on the neural component. Using Lyapunov theory and a small-gain analysis, we show that enforcing a Lipschitz bound on the learning component guarantees uniform ultimate boundedness of the closed-loop error dynamics. The proposed framework is validated on a quadrotor landing task subject to strong ground-effect disturbances across normal and out-of-distribution scenarios, demonstrating accuracy-robustness trade-off and greater operational reliability during training, deployment, and transfer compared with state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: A learning-enabled disturbance-rejection framework based on Neural Extended State Observer (Neural-ESO) with dual-pathway architecture combining neural network feedforward estimation and conventional ESO correction, proven stable via Lyapunov theory and small-gain analysis, and validated on quadrotor landing tasks with strong ground-effect disturbances.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based control methods rely on learned models once deployed, lacking robust disturbance rejection capabilities. A framework is needed that can handle disturbances effectively while maintaining reliability during training, deployment, and transfer.
AI.method: Dual-pathway architecture: (1) Predictive pathway uses a neural network to provide feedforward disturbance estimate for faster convergence, (2) Corrective pathway employs a conventional Extended State Observer (ESO) to compensate prediction errors and prevent over-reliance on the neural component. The learning component is enforced with a Lipschitz bound for stability analysis.
AI.result: Validated on quadrotor landing task subject to strong ground-effect disturbances across normal and out-of-distribution scenarios, demonstrating accuracy-robustness trade-off and greater operational reliability compared to state-of-the-art baselines during training, deployment, and transfer.
AI.conclusion: Using Lyapunov theory and small-gain analysis, enforcing a Lipschitz bound on the learning component guarantees uniform ultimate boundedness of the closed-loop error dynamics, proving the framework's stability and reliability across different operational scenarios.

title: UniLM-Nav: A Unified Framework for Zero-Shot Last-Mile Navigation
summary: Mobile manipulation requires a robot to navigate to a target object or receptacle and then perform intended manipulation. However, reaching the vicinity of the target does not guarantee a manipulation-ready base pose, a problem known as last-mile navigation. Prior methods for last-mile navigation either rely on manual pose annotation or task-specific training, limiting their scalability to open-vocabulary settings with fine-grained spatial constraints. We propose UniLM-Nav, a unified framework for zero-shot open-vocabulary last-mile navigation. UniLM-Nav decomposes last-mile navigation into view selection, task-conditioned affordance grounding, and geometry-aware base-pose reasoning, all resolved with a shared multimodal large language model (MLLM) backend. Specifically, UniLM-Nav first selects a reference view that best captures the target object or receptacle from recently collected observations. It then grounds task-relevant affordance point in the selected view and lifts the result into the robot-centric coordinate frame. Finally, conditioned on the grounded affordance, task context, and robot geometry, it infers a manipulation-ready base pose for the robot. We evaluate UniLM-Nav on the OVMM benchmark, where it outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method, MoTo, by 3.13 percentage points. Analyses show that the components of our method are crucial to final performance, and that the choice of MLLM also has a substantial effect. We further deploy UniLM-Nav on a Unitree B2 quadruped robot with a 6-DoF Unitree Z1 manipulator, validating its applicability to real-world mobile manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: UniLM-Nav is a unified framework for zero-shot open-vocabulary last-mile navigation in mobile manipulation, decomposing the problem into view selection, task-conditioned affordance grounding, and geometry-aware base-pose reasoning, all resolved by a shared multimodal large language model (MLLM) backend.
AI.motivation: Mobile manipulation requires robots to navigate to target objects and perform manipulation, but reaching the vicinity doesn't guarantee a manipulation-ready base pose (last-mile navigation problem). Prior methods rely on manual pose annotation or task-specific training, limiting scalability to open-vocabulary settings with fine-grained spatial constraints.
AI.method: UniLM-Nav decomposes last-mile navigation into three components: (1) view selection to capture the target object/receptacle from recent observations, (2) task-conditioned affordance grounding to identify task-relevant affordance points in the selected view, and (3) geometry-aware base-pose reasoning to infer a manipulation-ready base pose conditioned on grounded affordance, task context, and robot geometry. All three steps are resolved with a shared MLLM backend.
AI.result: On the OVMM benchmark, UniLM-Nav outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method MoTo by 3.13 percentage points. Analysis shows each component is crucial to performance, and the choice of MLLM significantly affects results. The method is successfully deployed on a Unitree B2 quadruped robot with a 6-DoF Unitree Z1 manipulator for real-world mobile manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: UniLM-Nav demonstrates that a unified MLLM-based approach can effectively solve the open-vocabulary last-mile navigation problem by decomposing it into view selection, affordance grounding, and base-pose reasoning. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks and validates its applicability to real-world mobile manipulation scenarios.

title: RynnWorld-Teleop: An Action-Conditioned World Model for Digital Teleoperation
summary: Scaling robot learning requires massive, diverse trajectory data, yet collection is currently bottlenecked by physical teleoperation, where every demonstration binds operator time to specific hardware and workspaces. We introduce digital teleoperation, a paradigm that decouples data collection from physical constraints by replacing the real robot with a generative world model. In this framework, an operator's hand-pose stream drives a robot-centric generative world model to synthesize high-fidelity egocentric videos from a single reference image. The recorded pose stream serves as an embodiment-agnostic action label transferable to any target robot via standard retargeting, yielding complete state-action trajectories for imitation learning independent of physical hardware. We instantiate this paradigm in RynnWorld-Teleop, a system that integrates depth-aware skeletal conditioning, progressive human-to-robot training on a video Diffusion Transformer, and streaming autoregressive distillation. This pipeline compresses the generative process into a single-pass inference, enabling 40+ FPS, real-time interactive generation on a single H100 GPU. Policies trained exclusively on RynnWorld-Teleop-generated data achieve effective zero-shot Sim2Real transfer across dexterous and diverse bimanual tasks. Moreover, augmenting real-world datasets with our digitally teleoperated data consistently improves success rates, demonstrating that RynnWorld-Teleop serves as a high-fidelity, scalable data engine for the next generation of robotic agents.

AI.tldr: Digital teleoperation uses generative world models to synthesize high-fidelity robot training data from human pose streams, enabling hardware-agnostic data collection at real-time speeds (40+ FPS) and achieving zero-shot Sim2Real transfer.
AI.motivation: Scaling robot learning requires massive, diverse trajectory data, but physical teleoperation is bottlenecked by physical constraints and operator time, limiting data collection efficiency.
AI.method: RynnWorld-Teleop integrates depth-aware skeletal conditioning, progressive human-to-robot training on a video Diffusion Transformer, and streaming autoregressive distillation. The system uses an operator's hand-pose stream to drive a robot-centric generative world model, synthesizing high-fidelity egocentric videos from a single reference image. The pose stream serves as embodiment-agnostic action labels transferable via standard retargeting.
AI.result: Policies trained exclusively on RynnWorld-Teleop-generated data achieve effective zero-shot Sim2Real transfer across dexterous and diverse bimanual tasks. Augmenting real-world datasets with digitally teleoperated data consistently improves success rates.
AI.conclusion: RynnWorld-Teleop serves as a high-fidelity, scalable data engine for the next generation of robotic agents, decoupling data collection from physical hardware constraints.

title: RynnWorld-4D: 4D Embodied World Models for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation in the open world requires not only recognizing what a scene looks like, but also anticipating how its 3D structure moves under interaction. We argue that synchronized RGB, depth, and optical flow, namely RGB-DF, provide a physically grounded representation that captures the underlying 4D dynamics of a scene. Compared to 2D pixel videos, this multi-modal synergy aligns visual appearance with geometric structure and temporal motion, creating a representation space significantly closer to the low-level end-effector actions demanded by robotic systems, thereby narrowing the gap between world prediction and policy learning. Building on this insight, we introduce RynnWorld-4D, a generative model that co-produces future RGB frames, depth maps, and optical flow from a single RGB-D image and a language instruction within one unified diffusion process. This 4D world model features a tri-branch architecture that integrates cross-modal attention with frame-wise 3D RoPE, ensuring that appearance, geometry, and motion evolve consistently. To supply training data at scale, we curate Rynn4DDataset 1.0, a massive dataset of over 254.4 million frames across egocentric human and robotic manipulation videos with high-quality pseudo-labels for depth and optical flow. We further propose RynnWorld-4D-Policy, an inverse dynamics head that consumes the internal 4D representations of RynnWorld-4D in a single forward pass, bypassing expensive multi-step denoising, to output robot actions in a closed-loop manner. Experiments show that RynnWorld-4D produces temporally and spatially coherent 4D predictions, and that RynnWorld-4D-Policy achieves state-of-the-art performance on real-world dexterous bimanual manipulation tasks, particularly excelling in tasks demanding spatial precision and temporal coordination.

AI.tldr: RynnWorld-4D is a 4D generative world model that predicts RGB frames, depth maps, and optical flow from RGB-D images and language instructions, with an integrated policy head for robotic manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation requires not only scene recognition but also anticipating 3D structure movement under interaction. RGB-DF (synchronized RGB, depth, and optical flow) provides a physically grounded representation that captures 4D dynamics, bridging the gap between world prediction and policy learning.
AI.method: RynnWorld-4D uses a tri-branch diffusion architecture with cross-modal attention and frame-wise 3D RoPE to co-produce RGB frames, depth maps, and optical flow. It's trained on Rynn4DDataset 1.0 (254.4 million frames from egocentric videos). RynnWorld-4D-Policy is an inverse dynamics head that consumes internal 4D representations to output robot actions in a single forward pass.
AI.result: The model produces temporally and spatially coherent 4D predictions. RynnWorld-4D-Policy achieves state-of-the-art performance on real-world dexterous bimanual manipulation tasks, particularly excelling in tasks requiring spatial precision and temporal coordination.
AI.conclusion: RGB-DF representation successfully narrows the gap between world prediction and policy learning, enabling effective robotic manipulation in open-world scenarios through synchronized multi-modal prediction and efficient policy learning.

title: Embodied Human-Robot Interaction via Acoustics: A MARL Approach with AcoustoBots for Spatial Data Physicalization
comment: This paper has been accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on Robotic System and Artificial Intelligence (RSAI 2026), 10-12 July, 2026, Tokyo, Japan
summary: Traditional data physicalization is often static and disconnected from real environments, limiting its ability to convey embodied spatial dynamics and engage users. To address this limitation, we present AcoustoBots, a mobile acoustophoretic data-physicalization platform in which TurtleBot3 robots carry upward-facing 8 x 8 ultrasonic phased arrays. Each array levitates a particle whose height (1-10 cm) encodes a local urban scalar value, such as population density, noise, or traffic. A MARL (Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning) policy based on the Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) algorithm, with centralized training and decentralized execution, selects collision-aware navigation actions, while a high-rate Gerchberg-Saxton-Phased Array of Transducers (GS-PAT) acoustic controller maintains trap stability and updates array phases to achieve the commanded height during motion. This creates a closed perception-display-action loop. We evaluate single-robot city-to-city traversal and dual-robot cooperative coverage on a 4 m x 3 m scaled UK map using PhaseSpace-based localization for repeatable multi-robot trials. Results show stable in-motion levitation and consistent, location-dependent height rendering, with task success rates of 90% and 80% for the single and dual-robot regimes, respectively, over 10 trials per regime, and low collision counts. These findings support acoustophoretic levitation as a simple, glanceable, robot-mediated communication cue for embodied human-robot interaction in spatial analytics.

AI.tldr: AcoustoBots is a mobile acoustophoretic data-physicalization platform where TurtleBot3 robots equipped with ultrasonic phased arrays levitate particles whose height (1-10 cm) encodes urban data values (population density, noise, traffic). Using MADDPG-based MARL for collision-aware navigation and GS-PAT acoustic control for in-motion levitation, the system achieves stable height rendering with 90% single-robot and 80% dual-robot task success rates.
AI.motivation: Traditional data physicalization is static and disconnected from real environments, limiting its ability to convey embodied spatial dynamics and engage users in spatial analytics applications.
AI.method: TurtleBot3 robots carry upward-facing 8×8 ultrasonic phased arrays that levitate particles whose height encodes urban scalar values. Navigation uses MADDPG-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (centralized training, decentralized execution) for collision-aware path planning, while a high-rate Gerchberg-Saxton-Phased Array of Transducers (GS-PAT) acoustic controller maintains trap stability and updates phases during motion. Evaluation uses PhaseSpace-based localization on a 4m×3m UK map with single-robot traversal and dual-robot cooperative coverage trials.
AI.result: The system achieves stable in-motion levitation and consistent, location-dependent height rendering. Over 10 trials per regime, task success rates are 90% for single-robot traversal and 80% for dual-robot cooperative coverage, with low collision counts.
AI.conclusion: Acoustophoretic levitation demonstrates potential as a simple, glanceable, robot-mediated communication cue for embodied human-robot interaction in spatial analytics, enabling dynamic data visualization integrated with physical environments.

title: Lift3D-VLA: Lifting VLA Models to 3D Geometry and Dynamics-Aware Manipulation
summary: Recently, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong generalization across diverse tasks. However, effective robotic manipulation in physical environments fundamentally requires geometric understanding and spatial reasoning. While some VLA approaches attempt to incorporate 3D information, they are constrained by limited data availability and geometric information loss in current 3D encoding pipelines, and fail to jointly capture 3D geometry and temporally structured actions in dynamic environments. To address these limitations, we introduce Lift3D-VLA, a unified VLA framework that equips models with explicit 3D point cloud reasoning and enables temporally coherent action generation. First, building upon our previous work Lift3D, an enhanced 2D model-lifting strategy is proposed to geometrically align 3D points with pretrained 2D positional embeddings. This design enables direct point-cloud encoding within the VLA vision encoder while minimizing spatial information loss. Based on explicit 3D inputs, we propose Geometry-Centric Masked Autoencoding (GC-MAE), a dual-objective self-supervised framework that reconstructs the current point cloud while predicting its future geometric evolution. This formulation allows the 2D vision encoder to internalize both 3D structure and physical dynamics. To fully exploit 3D representations, we further design layer-wise temporal action modeling, which leverages multiple layers of the LLM to collaboratively predict action chunks, enabling temporally consistent predictions. Across 22 simulated tasks and 8 real-world manipulation tasks, Lift3D-VLA achieves 10.8% and 11.1% higher mean success rates on MetaWorld and RLBench than the best-performing prior VLA methods, and outperforms the strongest real-world baseline by 4 percentage points, while exhibiting stronger generalization to out-of-distribution perturbations.

AI.tldr: Lift3D-VLA is a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that enhances robotic manipulation by incorporating explicit 3D point cloud reasoning and temporally coherent action generation through geometric alignment, dual-objective self-supervised learning, and layer-wise temporal action modeling.
AI.motivation: While VLA models demonstrate strong generalization, effective robotic manipulation requires geometric understanding and spatial reasoning. Existing 3D encoding approaches suffer from limited data availability and geometric information loss, and fail to jointly capture 3D geometry and temporally structured actions in dynamic environments.
AI.method: Lift3D-VLA employs three key innovations: 1) Enhanced 2D model-lifting strategy (based on Lift3D) to geometrically align 3D points with pretrained 2D positional embeddings for direct point-cloud encoding; 2) Geometry-Centric Masked Autoencoding (GC-MAE), a dual-objective self-supervised framework that reconstructs current point cloud while predicting its future geometric evolution; 3) Layer-wise temporal action modeling that leverages multiple LLM layers to collaboratively predict action chunks for temporal consistency.
AI.result: On 22 simulated tasks and 8 real-world manipulation tasks, Lift3D-VLA achieves 10.8% and 11.1% higher mean success rates on MetaWorld and RLBench respectively compared to best prior VLA methods, outperforms the strongest real-world baseline by 4 percentage points, and demonstrates stronger generalization to out-of-distribution perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Lift3D-VLA successfully addresses the limitations of current VLA approaches by incorporating explicit 3D point cloud reasoning and temporally coherent action generation, demonstrating that the combination of geometric alignment, dual-objective self-supervised learning, and layer-wise temporal modeling enables more effective robotic manipulation in both simulated and real-world environments.
